pests.name: Slugs and snails
pests.note_beginner: Slugs and snails chew ragged holes in viola leaves and flowers, mostly at night and in the cool, damp weather violas love. Hand-pick after dark, set out traps, or use iron-phosphate bait, and clear damp hiding spots near the plants.
pests.note_seasoned: The characteristic cool-season viola pest: slugs and snails rasp holes in foliage and bloom under the damp, mild conditions violas thrive in. Reduce harborage, hand-pick at night, and use traps or iron-phosphate baits; pressure is highest in shaded, mulched, irrigated beds.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.note_beginner: Tiny soft insects that cluster on new growth and buds and can spread viruses. A strong spray of water or insecticidal soap usually handles them.
pests.note_seasoned: Soft-bodied sap-feeders on tender growth and buds; cool-season colonies can build quickly and vector viruses. Hose off or treat with insecticidal soap, and conserve the ladybugs and hoverflies that feed on them.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.note_beginner: Very tiny pests that show up in hot, dry conditions late in the viola season and cause fine speckling on leaves. Spraying leaves with water and keeping plants watered helps.
pests.note_seasoned: Stippling and fine webbing under hot, dry conditions as the season warms; a late-season problem that coincides with the heat decline. Raise humidity with base watering and dislodge with water sprays; rarely worth treating on a fading planting.

pests.name: Foliage-feeding caterpillars
pests.note_beginner: Caterpillars sometimes chew viola leaves and flowers. Pick them off, or use a targeted Bt product if there are many.
pests.note_seasoned: Various caterpillars, including fritillary larvae that favor violets, chew foliage and bloom; usually cosmetic. Hand-pick, or apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) where populations warrant, leaving native fritillary larvae where butterflies are wanted.

diseases.name: Crown and root rot
diseases.note_beginner: The most common way violas are lost. The plant wilts, yellows, and collapses from the base, usually because the soil stayed warm and wet or did not drain well. Plant in well-drained soil, do not overwater, and start with healthy plants.
diseases.note_seasoned: Viola's signature killer: crown and root rots (black root rot from Thielaviopsis, plus Pythium and Phytophthora) favored by warm, wet, poorly drained soil and high pH. Plants wilt and collapse at the base. Management is cultural: excellent drainage, restrained watering, slightly acidic soil, healthy transplants, and rotating beds where rot has built up.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.note_beginner: A disease that shows as yellow blotches on top of leaves with a grayish fuzz underneath, worst in cool, wet weather. Space plants for airflow and keep the leaves dry.
diseases.note_seasoned: Cool, wet conditions favor downy mildew: angular yellow lesions above with sporulation beneath. Manage with spacing for airflow, base watering, morning irrigation, and sanitation of infected debris.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.note_beginner: A white, powdery coating on leaves, more common in crowded plantings. Give plants room for air to move and water the soil, not the leaves.
diseases.note_seasoned: A white fungal coating favored by crowding and moderate temperatures; cosmetic to moderate. Manage with spacing, airflow, and base watering rather than overhead wetting.

diseases.name: Leaf spots and anthracnose
diseases.note_beginner: Brown or dark spots on leaves, worse when leaves stay wet. Keep foliage dry, space plants out, and remove badly spotted leaves.
diseases.note_seasoned: Foliar spotting (including pansy leaf spot and anthracnose) spread by overhead wetness and splash; manage with base watering, spacing, morning irrigation, and sanitation of infected debris.

diseases.name: Gray mold (Botrytis blight)
diseases.note_beginner: A gray, fuzzy mold on faded flowers and damaged leaves in cool, damp weather. Remove spent blooms and dead leaves promptly.
diseases.note_seasoned: Botrytis blight grays and rots spent blooms and senescing tissue under cool, humid, still conditions. Deadhead promptly, improve airflow, and clear debris; it follows neglect of spent flowers.
